::: {.callout-note}
## What this is

A working draft of an interactive dynamic-programming matrix, written for
Sessions 4 and 5. It is not linked from the course notes and not in Canvas.
This page exists so that it can be looked at and argued with before it goes
anywhere students can reach.

The same widget already supplies the matrix figures on the Session 4 slides:
every matrix in block 2 of that deck is a screenshot of what is below, so the
projector and this page cannot drift apart.
:::

## Why bother

The matrix is the one thing in Session 4 that every student has to be able to
fill by hand, and it is the thing a static figure teaches worst. A figure can
assert that three candidates were compared and the largest kept. It cannot let
anyone get it wrong and find out why.

Three ways of using it, from watching to doing.

## 1 · Step through it

The blue cell is the one being decided. The three yellow cells are the only
ones it is allowed to look at, and each carries a badge with the value it
offers; the winning offer is green. That green badge is the `max` in the
recurrence, happening where the room can see it.

$$V(i,j) = \max \begin{cases} V(i-1,j-1) + s(x_i, y_j) \\ V(i-1,j) + g \\ V(i,j-1) + g \end{cases}$$

```{=html}
<div id="dp-step"></div>
<script>
renderDP("dp-step", {mode: "step", a: "GCAT", b: "GAC", match: 1, mismatch: -1, gap: -1});
</script>
```

This is the GCAT against GAC example of Table 4.1, with match $+1$, mismatch
$-1$ and gap $-1$ — the same numbers as the lecture and the notebook.

## 2 · Guess the next value

Everything above and to the left is filled in already. Work out the blue cell
and type it. Whether the answer is right or wrong, the full `max(...)` is shown
afterwards, and the widget says so when two predecessors tie, which is the
point students most often miss.

```{=html}
<div id="dp-guess"></div>
<script>
renderDP("dp-guess", {mode: "guess", a: "GCAT", b: "GAC", match: 1, mismatch: -1, gap: -1, questions: 4});
</script>
```

## 3 · Fill the whole matrix

Every cell is yours to type. **Check the matrix** marks each one, and the
traceback and the alignment appear once the grid is right. This is the lab
exercise, done in a browser rather than on paper, and marked instantly.

```{=html}
<div id="dp-fill"></div>
<script>
renderDP("dp-fill", {mode: "fill", a: "GCAT", b: "GAC", match: 1, mismatch: -1, gap: -1});
</script>
```

## It is not only Session 4

The same engine takes a substitution matrix instead of a match/mismatch pair,
and a zero floor instead of none. Below is Smith–Waterman on protein with
BLOSUM62 and a gap of $-8$: the local case, where the floor of zero is a
*fourth* alternative and gets a badge of its own in the cell being decided.
That is the only place local differs from global, and it is invisible in a
static figure.

```{=html}
<div id="dp-local"></div>
<script>
renderDP("dp-local", {mode: "step", a: "HEAGAWGHEE", b: "PAWHEAE", scoring: "blosum62", gap: -8, local: true});
</script>
```

Viterbi is the same recurrence with max-plus over log probabilities, so the
profile-HMM half of Session 5 is a fourth mode rather than a second program.

## Try your own

Everything above is fixed, so that the prose can describe it. This one is not.

Type a pair of sequences, or set a length and press **New pair** — the second
sequence is a mutated copy of the first rather than an independent draw, because
two random strings align into noise and teach nothing. Switching **Alphabet**
between DNA and Protein also switches the scoring, since match/mismatch on
protein wastes the demonstration and BLOSUM62 on four nucleotides is meaningless.
Gap cost, global or local, and the mode can all be changed without losing the
sequences.

```{=html}
<div id="dp-play"></div>
<script>
renderDP("dp-play", {
  controls: true,
  modes: ["step", "guess", "fill"],
  mode: "step",
  a: "TGCATTA", b: "GCATTAC", match: 3, mismatch: -1, gap: -2
});
</script>
```

Anything on this page can be set in the same way from a session page: the
settings bar is one flag on the call, so a chapter can show a fixed example
while the lab lets students change it.

## What we would like to know

1. **Does it belong in the lecture, the lab, or only the notes?** The slides
   already use it as a build-up. Whether a live demo is worth the minutes it
   costs in the room is a different question.
2. **Is GCAT against GAC the right example to keep?** It is small enough to do
   in the room and it matches Table 4.1, but it has a tie in it, which is
   either a feature or a distraction.
3. **For Session 5, is BLOSUM62 with a linear gap enough**, or does the affine
   gap need to be visible too? Affine means three matrices, and three matrices
   on one screen may teach less than it shows.

## Provenance

Written for this course, from the recurrence, in plain JavaScript with no
dependencies. Lukas Käll's
[alignviz](https://github.com/statisticalbiotechnology/alignviz) (Apache-2.0)
does the stepping well and is worth a look, but it is a Streamlit server with
no substitution matrix and no answer checking; nothing here is derived from it.
